title: The Shutdown Build: Why a Manufacturer's Final Production Run Before Christmas Doesn't Turn Into Cash Until February
excerpt: Running the line harder before a Christmas shutdown feels like good management. For many manufacturers, it also ties up cash in finished stock that will not turn into cash until February.
content:
Manufacturing floors across Brisbane, Sydney and Melbourne tend to run at their hardest in the final weeks before Christmas. Customers want their last orders filled before everyone shuts down for the break, so the production schedule tightens and the line runs harder than at almost any other point in the year. From the outside, a factory at full capacity in late November looks like exactly the position every manufacturer wants to be in.

The pattern underneath it is less comfortable. That final run has to cover more than the orders already confirmed. Most manufacturers also build a buffer of finished goods to keep key customers supplied through the weeks the factory is closed, which means paying for materials, labour and freight well before the shutdown even starts. The cash those goods represent does not arrive until the stock ships, the invoice is raised, and the customer's payment terms run their course. For a business trading on thirty to sixty day terms, that gap often lands somewhere in February.

None of this looks like a mistake while it is happening. Running the line harder, building the buffer stock, protecting the customer relationship, every one of those calls is the right one on its own. The problem is that nobody usually adds up what all of those right decisions cost in cash at the one point in the year the business can least afford a surprise.

The Run Before the Break

Building finished goods stock ahead of a shutdown spreads overhead over more units in the short term, which can make the month look like a strong one on the P&L. It does the opposite to the balance sheet. Raw materials, direct labour and freight all get paid for weeks before the matching sale is confirmed, and that stock sits as working capital rather than cash until a customer actually takes delivery. Freight itself gets harder and more expensive to book in the fortnight before Christmas, as every importer, retailer and manufacturer on the east coast tries to move goods through the same ports, depots and carriers at once, which adds a further cost to a production run that was already funded well ahead of its revenue.

The buffer is rarely spread evenly across the customer base either. A handful of key accounts usually drive most of the pre-Christmas surge, which means the cash tied up in that final run is concentrated against the payment habits of a small number of customers rather than averaged across many. If one of those accounts runs its own cash tight over the break and pays late, the manufacturer absorbs that delay on top of everything else already funded ahead of the shutdown.

The Costs That Don't Stop When the Line Does

A factory lease, equipment finance and insurance do not take the same break the production line does. Neither does the portion of salaried staff most manufacturers retain over the shutdown to manage maintenance, security and the restart. For the two to four weeks the plant is closed, those fixed costs keep running without a single new invoice being raised to offset them, at exactly the point the final pre-Christmas invoices are still working their way through a customer's payment cycle rather than clearing into the business's account.

Modelling the Return, Not Just the Break

The manufacturers who move through January calmly are rarely the ones who had the quietest shutdown. They are the ones who knew, before the line stopped, exactly when the cash from that last production run would land, what it would cost to restart in the new year once supplier lead times and casual staff availability came back into play, and whether a short-term facility was worth arranging in advance rather than mid crisis. A 13-Week Cash Flow Build run across the shutdown and the weeks either side of it turns that uncertainty into a specific weekly number, rather than a hope that the bank balance holds. The same forecast earns its keep again at restart, when the business is paying wages and chasing suppliers before a single dollar from the new year's production has come back in.

Restarting also has its own cost, separate from the shutdown itself. Suppliers who were happy to extend terms in a normal month often tighten them in the weeks after their own Christmas break, and raw material lead times can blow out if a key supplier has also been closed. A business that has modelled the shutdown but not the restart can find itself needing cash for the January reorder at the same time the February customer payments it was counting on still have not cleared.

The Christmas order book is good news for almost every manufacturer. What decides whether the shutdown feels calm or tight is whether the cash gap it creates was modelled back in November or discovered somewhere in the new year. Manufacturers who want that clarity before the line stops are usually better served building the cash flow discipline around the shutdown now, while there is still time to arrange whatever buffer the forecast says is needed, rather than once the factory floor in Melbourne or Brisbane has already gone quiet for the break.

faqs.q: Why do manufacturers often run short on cash straight after a Christmas shutdown?
faqs.a: The final production run before a shutdown usually includes a buffer of finished goods built to keep key customers supplied through the break, and that stock is paid for in materials, labour and freight well before the matching invoice clears. On thirty to sixty day customer terms, the cash from that run often does not land until February, right as the business is also funding the cost of restarting the line.

faqs.q: How much finished goods stock should a manufacturer build before a Christmas shutdown?
faqs.a: There is no single figure that fits every business, since it depends on how long the shutdown runs and how quickly customers draw down stock once the factory reopens. The more useful question is what that buffer costs in cash before a single unit ships, and whether the business has actually modelled that outlay against when the matching sales will clear, rather than estimating it from habit.

faqs.q: Do fixed costs like leases and equipment finance keep running during a factory shutdown?
faqs.a: Yes. A factory lease, equipment finance and insurance are contracted obligations that continue regardless of whether the production line is running, and most manufacturers also retain some salaried staff over the break for maintenance, security and restart preparation. None of those costs pause just because trading has, which is part of why the shutdown period puts more pressure on cash than it does on the P&L.

faqs.q: How long does it typically take customer payments to clear after a pre-Christmas production run?
faqs.a: Most manufacturers trade on thirty to sixty day terms, and a customer's own payment cycle often adds further delay on top of that, particularly over a period when their own accounts team is also working through a Christmas shutdown. For stock shipped in the first half of December, it is common for the matching cash not to clear until February.

faqs.q: What is the best way to forecast cash flow through a manufacturing shutdown period?
faqs.a: A rolling weekly forecast that covers the final production run, the shutdown itself and the weeks needed to restart gives a far more accurate picture than a monthly view, because the timing mismatch between paying for stock and collecting for it plays out week by week, not month by month. A 13-Week Cash Flow Build is built specifically for this kind of concentrated, predictable cash event.

faqs.q: Should a manufacturer arrange a short-term facility before a Christmas shutdown, not during it?
faqs.a: Arranging finance ahead of the shutdown gives a lender time to properly assess the request and gives the business leverage on timing and terms it will not have mid crisis. Reviewing cash flow discipline around the shutdown each November, well before the line stops, is the difference between a planned buffer and a request made under pressure.
